points.title: Place as a geographical idea
points.brief: A place is a part of the Earth's surface that people give meaning to, such as a home, a town or a sacred site, and places shape people's sense of belonging.

points.title: Space and where things are
points.brief: Space is about where features are found and how they are spread out, and how one location relates to other places nearby.

points.title: Environment as a geographical idea
points.brief: The environment is the natural and built surroundings that people live in, which natural processes and human activity both change.

points.title: Interconnection between people and places
points.brief: Interconnection means people, places and environments are linked, so a change in one, such as a new road, affects the others.

points.title: The parts of a map
points.brief: A useful map has a border, orientation (a north arrow), a legend, a title and a scale, often remembered as BOLTS.

points.title: Area references
points.brief: A four-figure area reference names a grid square by its easting first, then its northing, to locate a feature roughly.

points.title: Grid references
points.brief: A six-figure grid reference splits each grid square into tenths to give a more exact position, again easting first.

points.title: Measuring distance with a map scale
points.brief: A line scale or ratio scale turns a distance measured on the map into the real distance on the ground.

points.title: Contour lines and slope
points.brief: Contour lines join places of the same height. Lines close together show a steep slope and lines far apart show a gentle one.

points.title: Choosing and reading graphs
points.brief: Column, bar, line and picture graphs suit different data, and a line graph shows how something changes over time.

points.title: The fieldwork process
points.brief: Fieldwork follows steps, from asking a geographical question to collecting and recording data, finding what it shows and sharing the findings.

points.title: Satellite images and GPS
points.brief: Satellite images show places from above and how they change over time, and GPS uses satellites to find an exact location.

points.title: Geographic information systems
points.brief: A GIS layers different kinds of data on one digital map, such as roads, rivers and population, so patterns can be compared.

points.title: Landscapes and landforms
points.brief: A landscape is a whole area of land with its own look, such as a coast or a desert. A landform is a single feature in it, such as a cliff or a sand dune.

points.title: Types of landscapes
points.brief: Landscapes include mountain, coastal, riverine, desert, rainforest and volcanic landscapes, each with its own landforms.

points.title: Weathering
points.brief: Weathering breaks down rock where it sits, through physical processes such as heating and freezing, chemical processes and living things such as roots.

points.title: Erosion and deposition
points.brief: Erosion carries broken rock away by water, wind or ice, and deposition drops it somewhere else, building landforms such as beaches and deltas.

points.title: Rivers shaping the land
points.brief: Rivers cut valleys and gorges in their upper course and drop sediment to make floodplains and deltas lower down.

points.title: Coasts shaping the land
points.brief: Waves erode headlands into cliffs, caves, arches and stacks, and carry sand along the shore to build beaches and spits.

points.title: Tectonic forces and mountains
points.brief: Plates of the Earth's crust move slowly, and where they push together they fold rock up into mountains and cause volcanoes.

points.title: People changing landscapes
points.brief: Human activities such as mining, farming, building dams and clearing land change landforms, sometimes faster than natural processes.

points.title: Why landscapes matter
points.brief: People value landscapes for different reasons, such as beauty, recreation, farming, tourism, cultural meaning and spiritual meaning.

points.title: Aboriginal Peoples' connection to Country
points.brief: For Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples, landscapes are part of Country, tied to identity, stories and law, as Uluru is for the Anangu.

points.title: Caring for Country
points.brief: Aboriginal Peoples have managed and cared for landscapes for tens of thousands of years, through practices such as cultural burning and protecting sacred sites.

points.title: Protecting landscapes at different scales
points.brief: Landscapes are protected locally by councils, nationally through national parks, and globally through World Heritage listing.

points.title: What a geomorphic hazard is
points.brief: A geomorphic hazard is a natural event in the land, such as an earthquake, volcanic eruption, landslide or tsunami, that can harm people.

points.title: What causes earthquakes and tsunamis
points.brief: Earthquakes happen when stress builds where plates meet and the rock suddenly slips. An earthquake under the sea can push up a tsunami.

points.title: What causes volcanic eruptions
points.brief: Molten rock called magma rises where plates pull apart or one plate slides under another, and erupts as lava, ash and gas.

points.title: What causes landslides
points.brief: Landslides happen when a slope gives way, often after heavy rain, an earthquake, or clearing the plants whose roots hold the soil.

points.title: Staying safe and responding to geomorphic hazards
points.brief: People stay safe by following warnings and drills, such as drop, cover and hold on, and communities respond with building rules, warning systems and recovery help.

points.title: Liveability
points.brief: Liveability is how well a place meets people's needs for a good life, such as safety, services, jobs, housing and a healthy environment.

points.title: Perceptions of a place
points.brief: People see the same place differently depending on their age, culture and experience, so one person's ideal place is not another's.

points.title: Why people live where they do
points.brief: People choose where to live because of family, jobs, cost of housing, lifestyle, climate and cultural ties to a place.

points.title: Measuring liveability with data
points.brief: Liveability can be compared with data such as crime rates, travel times, house prices and access to parks, and surveys of what residents think.

points.title: Connections to a local area
points.brief: People and communities feel connected to a place through family, friends, culture, history and the places they gather, which makes it feel like home.

points.title: Access to services and facilities
points.brief: Schools, hospitals, shops, public transport and internet access make a place more liveable, and remote places often have fewer of them.

points.title: Physical influences on liveability
points.brief: Climate, natural hazards, landforms and access to water and green space affect how comfortable and safe a place is to live in.

points.title: Human influences on liveability
points.brief: Crime, traffic, pollution, noise, housing costs and job opportunities are human influences that make a place more or less liveable.

points.title: Ways to improve liveability
points.brief: Places become more liveable through better transport, more parks and trees, safer streets, affordable housing and community facilities.

points.title: Caring for Country and liveability
points.brief: Caring for Country supports the health, culture and wellbeing of Aboriginal communities, and knowledge of Country can make places better for everyone.

points.title: Community action on liveability
points.brief: Local initiatives such as community gardens, clean-up days, youth spaces and council consultations get people involved in improving their area.

points.title: How people use water
points.brief: People use water every day for drinking, cooking, washing and gardens, and in farming, industry and making electricity.

points.title: Sources of water
points.brief: Fresh water comes from rivers, lakes, dams and groundwater, and also from rainwater tanks, desalination plants and recycled water.

points.title: Where the world's water is
points.brief: Most of the Earth's water is salty ocean, and most fresh water is locked in ice or underground, so only a tiny share is easy to reach.

points.title: The water cycle
points.brief: Water evaporates, condenses into clouds, falls as precipitation, and runs off over land or soaks into the ground before returning to the sea.

points.title: How people affect water quality
points.brief: Farm runoff, sewage, rubbish, industrial waste and stormwater carry pollutants into rivers, lakes and the sea.

points.title: Causes of water scarcity
points.brief: Water scarcity comes from low or unreliable rainfall, drought, overuse and pollution, and from people being unable to afford or reach clean water.

points.title: Rainfall variability in Australia
points.brief: Australia is the driest inhabited continent, and its rainfall changes a lot from year to year, so droughts and floods both happen.

points.title: Managing water sustainably
points.brief: Schools, homes and communities save water with tanks, water-wise gardens, fixing leaks, shorter showers and reusing grey water.

points.title: Aboriginal Peoples caring for water Country
points.brief: Aboriginal Peoples care for rivers, waterholes and wetlands as part of Country, guided by knowledge passed down over generations, such as fish traps at Brewarrina.

points.title: Types of water and weather hazards
points.brief: Hydrological hazards involve water, such as floods. Atmospheric hazards come from the weather, such as cyclones, severe storms, droughts and heatwaves.

points.title: What causes floods
points.brief: Floods happen when heavy or long rain makes rivers overflow or water collects faster than the ground and drains can take it away.

points.title: What causes tropical cyclones
points.brief: Tropical cyclones form over warm seas, where rising moist air feeds a spinning storm with very strong winds and heavy rain.

points.title: Early warning systems
points.brief: The Bureau of Meteorology and emergency services use forecasts, flood gauges, alert levels and phone messages to warn people early.

points.title: Staying safe in floods and storms
points.brief: People stay safe by having an emergency plan and kit, never driving through floodwater, and following the advice of the SES.

points.title: Personal connections
points.brief: People connect with family and friends in person, by phone and online, and these links can stretch to other countries.

points.title: Transport connecting people to goods
points.brief: Roads, railways, shipping and planes move people and goods, connecting places to the things they need.

points.title: Digital connections to goods and services
points.brief: The internet lets people shop online, stream, bank and use services from anywhere, which changes how places connect.

points.title: Staying safe online
points.brief: Cyber safety means protecting personal details, spotting scams and fake shops, using strong passwords and paying on secure sites.

points.title: Goods and services in trade
points.brief: Goods are things you can touch, such as food and phones. Services are work done for people, such as tourism, education and streaming.

points.title: Why places trade
points.brief: Places trade because no place can make everything it needs, so they sell what they make well and buy what they lack.

points.title: Access to goods and services
points.brief: Income, distance, transport, internet access and where people live affect which goods and services they can get.

points.title: Australia's trade
points.brief: Australia exports resources such as iron ore, coal and gas, farm products and education, and imports cars, fuel and electronics.

points.title: Effects of trade on places
points.brief: Trade can build ports and towns and bring jobs, but it can also harm environments through mining, shipping and transport emissions.

points.title: Impacts of producing goods
points.brief: Making goods uses land, water, energy and raw materials, and can cause pollution and habitat loss where they are made.

points.title: Impacts of consuming goods
points.brief: Buying and using goods creates waste, such as packaging, clothes and electronics thrown away, which ends up in landfill or the ocean.

points.title: Sustainable production practices
points.brief: Sustainable practices include using renewable energy, recycling materials, reducing packaging and fair trade that pays workers fairly.

points.title: Responsible consumption
points.brief: People can cut the effects of what they buy by reducing, reusing, repairing and recycling, and by choosing products made sustainably.
